splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in the Sentencing Guidelines or criminal statutes.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's or an agency's interpretation of an ambiguous guideline or criminal statute, or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This matters because it determines whether ambiguities in criminal sentencing provisions are resolved in favor of the government (via deference) or the defendant (via lenity).

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity takes precedence over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, meaning ambiguities must be resolved in the defendant's favor.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference applies even in the criminal context, and an agency's or Commission's reasonable interpretation of an ambiguous provision controls over the rule of lenity.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses (conspiracy, attempt, aiding and abetting) in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is entitled to deference when the guideline text itself does not mention inchoate offenses.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether commentary expanding the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include inchoate offenses like conspiracy is a valid, binding interpretation of the guideline or impermissibly expands its scope. This affects whether defendants with prior conspiracy drug convictions qualify as career offenders with significantly higher sentencing ranges.

positions.label: Commentary is binding
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 is an authoritative interpretation of the guideline entitled to Stinson/Kisor deference, and thus inchoate offenses qualify as controlled substance offenses for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary is not binding
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, making Application Note 1 an impermissible expansion rather than an interpretation, and thus inchoate offenses do not qualify as controlled substance offenses.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to disqualify a defendant) or disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies).
splits.description: Circuits are deeply split on whether 'and' in § 3553(f)(1) means a defendant must meet all three listed criminal-history criteria to be disqualified from safety-valve relief, or whether meeting any one criterion is sufficient. This split leads to dramatically different sentencing outcomes for drug defendants depending on the circuit.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive (all three required to disqualify)
positions.summary: Holds that a defendant is disqualified from safety-valve relief only if all three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) are met, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive (any one criterion disqualifies)
positions.summary: Holds that meeting any one of the three criminal-history criteria in § 3553(f)(1) is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines (U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) or § 2K2.1) when the state schedule criminalizes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the Guidelines' definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance underlying a state conviction to also be federally scheduled, or whether any state-law drug offense qualifies regardless of federal scheduling. This affects base offense levels and career-offender status for many defendants with state drug priors.

positions.label: No federal-schedule limitation required
positions.summary: Holds that the Guidelines broadly define 'controlled substance offense' to include state-law drug offenses regardless of whether the particular substance is federally scheduled, because the text refers to offenses under 'state law' without limitation.

positions.label: Federal-schedule limitation applies
positions.summary: Holds that a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' only if the underlying substance is also controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's amendments to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c) stacking provisions) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A), and whether the Sentencing Commission's policy statement (U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6)) permitting this exceeds its statutory authority.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether non-retroactive statutory changes in sentencing law can support compassionate release motions. Some circuits hold that such changes can never contribute to an extraordinary and compelling reason, while others hold they can. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment purporting to authorize such relief has deepened the split over the Commission's authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in sentencing law cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for sentence reduction, and the Sentencing Commission lacks authority to override Congress's decision not to make changes retroactive.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes can support compassionate release
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in sentencing law may be considered, alone or in combination with other factors, as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether federal prisoners must bring challenges to the conditions or execution of their confinement (as opposed to the fact or duration) exclusively through habeas corpus under 28 U.S.C. § 2241, or whether they may also pursue civil rights claims (e.g., Bivens actions).
splits.description: A longstanding circuit split exists over whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging conditions or execution of confinement, or whether such claims may also be brought through other civil actions. This affects prisoners seeking to challenge BOP decisions such as First Step Act time-credit calculations and prerelease custody determinations.

positions.label: Habeas is not the exclusive remedy for conditions claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to conditions of confinement (as distinct from fact or duration) may be brought through civil rights actions and are not limited to habeas corpus.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy for execution-of-sentence claims
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to BOP decisions affecting the execution of a sentence, including prerelease custody and time credits, must be brought through habeas corpus rather than civil rights actions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of a debtor's asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to the debtor upon good-faith conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between filing a Chapter 13 petition and converting to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. This split significantly affects debtors who convert in good faith, as it determines whether a trustee can liquidate the appreciated value.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that the broad definition of 'property of the estate' under § 541(a) means post-petition appreciation in asset value is part of the estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that under § 348(f)(1)(A), post-petition, pre-conversion appreciation in property value belongs to the debtor upon good-faith conversion, consistent with the statute's structure and legislative history designed to protect good-faith converting debtors.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may impose sentences at supervised release revocation hearings for the purpose of punishing the defendant for the violation, or only for the purposes specified in 18 U.S.C. § 3583(e) and § 3553(a).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether punishment for the supervised release violation itself is a permissible sentencing purpose at revocation. Some circuits allow express consideration of punishment, while others hold the statutory framework limits sentencing to non-punitive purposes like deterrence and public protection.

positions.label: Punishment is a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly punish defendants for violations of supervised release conditions when imposing revocation sentences.

positions.label: Punishment is not a permissible purpose
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release revocation sentences should not be imposed for purposes of punishment but rather for the statutory purposes of deterrence, public protection, and rehabilitation.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the time to appeal a denial of attorney's fees under the Hyde Amendment follows the civil appeal deadline (30 days) or the criminal appeal deadline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (subject to the 30-day civil appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (subject to the 14-day criminal appeal deadline). This affects whether defendants' appeals of fee denials are timely.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, and therefore the 30-day civil appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(a) applies. This is the majority view.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Manchester Farming P'ship

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment fee motion is part of the criminal case, and the 14-day criminal appeal deadline under Fed. R. App. P. 4(b) applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the timing for when actuarial assumptions used to calculate employer withdrawal liability from multiemployer pension plans must be set. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations because the timing directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected before the statutory measurement date (end of the prior plan year), preventing the use of post-date assumptions that could increase liability.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that the actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, as the statute does not require all assumptions to be locked in before year-end.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending the period of court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. This affects thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled during periods of absconding, extending the court's authority to revoke supervised release beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that supervised release is not tolled during absconding because there is no statutory authorization for tolling, and the court's jurisdiction expires at the end of the stated term.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 28 U.S.C. § 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing successive motions under 28 U.S.C. § 2255.
splits.description: There is a 6-to-3 circuit split on whether federal prisoners face the additional gatekeeping requirement of § 2244(b)(1) — which categorically bars claims previously presented — when filing successive § 2255 motions, or whether they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s separate requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new rule of constitutional law.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners filing successive § 2255 motions, imposing a categorical bar in addition to § 2255(h)'s requirements.

positions.label: § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1) does not apply to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting rules. The outcome affects whether candidates can challenge mail-in voting procedures, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices before an election takes place.

positions.label: Standing exists for candidates
positions.summary: Holds that candidates for federal office have Article III standing to challenge state election laws that may affect the outcome of their races, including laws governing mail-in ballot deadlines.

positions.label: Standing is lacking for candidates
positions.summary: Holds that candidates do not automatically have Article III standing to challenge state election laws and must demonstrate a concrete, particularized injury beyond a generalized interest in lawful election procedures.

circuits.name: Seventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing private medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine.
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable as a collateral order because medical privacy is a value of sufficiently 'high order.' This raises questions about the scope of the collateral order doctrine that may differ from other circuits' approaches to similar privacy-related interlocutory appeals.

positions.label: Immediately appealable as collateral order
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of high order that cannot be effectively vindicated after final judgment.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal are not immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because the privacy interest can be adequately protected through other means such as protective orders or appeal after final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments?
splits.description: The Supreme Court granted certiorari to review the Second Circuit's approach to legal questions about discrimination liability and remedies in business establishments, indicating a circuit split or unsettled question warranting review. The decision may impact hospitality, retail, and service industries nationwide.

positions.label: Second Circuit approach
positions.summary: Applied legal standards for discrimination or unfair treatment claims in hospitality contexts that the Supreme Court found sufficiently problematic or divergent to warrant review.

positions.label: Contrary approach
positions.summary: Other circuits apply different standards for evaluating discrimination claims in business establishments, creating the split that led to certiorari.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state law categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violates the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated sex-based biological advantages, and whether as-applied equal protection challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.
splits.description: Circuits are divided on whether categorical bans on transgender athlete participation survive intermediate scrutiny when applied to individuals who have undergone medical transition. The case also raises the broader question of whether sex-based classifications affecting transgender individuals warrant heightened scrutiny.

positions.label: Categorical ban violates Equal Protection as applied
positions.summary: Holds that a categorical ban fails intermediate scrutiny as applied to transgender women who have medically mitigated biological advantages, because the state has not shown the ban is substantially related to its interest in competitive fairness for this subclass.

positions.label: Categorical ban does not violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that biological sex-based classifications in athletics are substantially related to the important governmental interest in fair competition and the safety of female athletes, even as applied to transgender women.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
